stem: A 12-month-old child on day 2 of bronchiolitis has oxygen saturations of 90% on room air and improves to 96% with supplemental oxygen. What is the best next management step?

options.text: Low flow oxygen via nasal prongs
High flow oxygen via nasal prongs

explanation: In bronchiolitis, the first-line management for hypoxaemia is supplemental oxygen, typically by low-flow nasal prongs, with escalation to high-flow nasal cannula or CPAP only if there is persistent work of breathing, ongoing hypoxaemia, or clinical deterioration despite standard oxygen therapy. This child’s saturation corrects with oxygen, so low-flow nasal prongs are the best option among those given.

citations.source: Agency for Clinical Innovation, NSW Health
citations.title: Bronchiolitis (suspected) | Paediatric ECAT protocol

rationale: The safest repair is to preserve the core clinical concept: an infant with bronchiolitis and mild hypoxaemia who responds to oxygen should receive low-flow oxygen first. Australian guidance places nasal prong oxygen as standard initial therapy, with HFNC/CPAP as escalation if needed.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Low-flow nasal prongs are the usual initial oxygen delivery method for mild hypoxaemia in bronchiolitis.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. High-flow nasal cannula is generally reserved for children who do not improve adequately with standard oxygen or who have more significant respiratory distress.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. CPAP is an escalation therapy for more severe respiratory compromise, not first-line for uncomplicated bronchiolitis with oxygen-responsive desaturation.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Intubation and ventilation are reserved for impending or established respiratory failure.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. A simple face mask is usually less suitable than nasal prongs in infants and is not the preferred initial oxygen delivery method for this presentation.

evidenceSources.title: Bronchiolitis
evidenceSources.supports: Bronchiolitis management includes supplemental oxygen when needed; high-flow nasal prong therapy is an escalation option rather than first-line for a child whose oxygenation improves with standard oxygen

evidenceSources.title: Bronchiolitis (suspected) | Paediatric ECAT protocol
evidenceSources.organization: Agency for Clinical Innovation, NSW Health
evidenceSources.supports: If oxygen saturations remain below 90% following oxygen therapy, prepare for humidified high-flow nasal cannula; this supports low-flow oxygen first and escalation only if needed

evidenceSources.title: Bronchiolitis – Emergency management in children
evidenceSources.supports: Bronchiolitis oxygen targets and escalation to HFNC/CPAP when standard oxygen is insufficient
